chapterTitle: Ch 44. Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.title: Rigidity assumption

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Any set of elements undergoing a 2D transformation with a unique interpretation as a rigid body moving in space should be interpreted as such a body in motion.
concepts.content: The rigidity assumption, introduced by Shimon Ullman in 1979, states: "Any set of elements undergoing a two dimensional transformation which has a unique interpretation as a rigid body moving in space should be interpreted as such a body in motion." This principle is fundamental to the problem of structure from motion (SFM), allowing for the 3D reconstruction of objects based on their movement.
concepts.motivation_md: The rigidity assumption provides a necessary constraint to solve the otherwise ill-posed problem of recovering 3D structure from 2D motion. Without assuming objects are rigid, an infinite number of non-rigid deformations could explain any 2D image sequence.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes that 2D transformations representing a possible rigid 3D motion should be interpreted as such.

key_passage.text: Any set of elements undergoing a two dimensional transformation which has a unique interpretation as a rigid body moving in space should be interpreted as such a body in motion.

concepts.title: Tomasi and Kanade SFM algorithm

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: An early structure from motion algorithm that uses keypoint trajectories under parallel projection to recover 3D point locations.
concepts.content: One of the first algorithms for structure from motion for rigid bodies was introduced by Tomasi and Kanade. For simplicity, their approach assumed parallel projection (orthographic camera) instead of perspective projection. The algorithm takes as input a video sequence captured by a moving camera looking at a static scene. The video is first processed by extracting keypoints and tracking them over time. The input to the reconstruction algorithm is the keypoint trajectories and the output is the 3D locations of those points with respect to a reference world-coordinate system, usually defined by the first frame in the video. This model was later extended by Sturm and Triggs to handle perspective projection.
concepts.motivation_md: This algorithm was developed to provide a systematic way to recover 3D scene geometry from a continuous video stream by tracking specific points over time.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses keypoint trajectories from a video sequence as input.

concepts.title: General Multiview SFM

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: General SFM reconstructs 3D scenes from multiple images taken by different cameras without assumptions about camera placement.
concepts.content: The task of SFM became more general, and instead of focusing on one moving camera, SFM was applied to the problem of reconstructing the 3D scene even from multiple images taken by different cameras and making no assumption about the placement of the cameras. Work by Snavely et al. showed how one could produce spectacular registrations and camera pose estimates of images taken with many different cameras, such as reconstructing famous buildings from pictures taken by tourists.
concepts.motivation_md: General multiview SFM allows for 3D reconstruction from unstructured image collections, such as internet photo sets, where camera parameters and positions are unknown and inconsistent.
concepts.recap_md: - Reconstructs 3D scenes from multiple, uncoordinated cameras.

concepts.title: Sparse SFM

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Sparse SFM recovers the 3D structure of a scene and camera locations from a set of images with overlapping content.
concepts.content:
Given a set of $M$ images with overlapping content, the goal of sparse SFM is to recover the 3D structure of the scene and the location of the camera for each image.

The bowl has a rough texture that might also allow for enough keypoints to be present along its surface. The images have $3,024 \times 4,032$ pixels.

Eight pictures taken in a plaza in Palma de Mallorca, Spain. The images have $3,024 \times 4,032$ pixels.

In the sparse SFM problem, we consider that in the scene there are $N$ distinct points (where $N$ is smaller than the number of pixels on each image) that are matched across $M$ different views. We denote the $N$ 3D points as $\mathbf{P}_i$. For each of the $M$ views, we denote the projection of point $\mathbf{P}_i$ as seen by camera $j$ by $\mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i$. Each view has camera parameters ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$, ${\mathbf R}^{(j)}$, and ${\mathbf T}^{(j)}$. The goal is to recover 3D points $\mathbf{P}_i$, the intrinsic camera parameters ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$, and the extrinsic camera parameters ${\mathbf R}^{(j)}$ and ${\mathbf T}^{(j)}$ for each camera $j$ given the set of corresponding 2D points $\mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i$.

Assuming calibrated cameras where ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}$ is known, we have $3N$ unknowns for the 3D points and $6(M-1)-1$ unknowns for the extrinsic parameters of $M-1$ cameras (assuming the first camera is at the origin). With $2NM$ observations, a solution is possible when $$2NM \geq 3N + 6(M-1)-1$$
concepts.motivation_md: Sparse SFM provides a mathematical framework to reconstruct 3D geometry using only a small set of identifiable feature points rather than every pixel, making the computation more efficient and robust to noise.
concepts.recap_md: - Recovers 3D points $\mathbf{P}_i$ and camera parameters ${\mathbf K}^{(j)}, {\mathbf R}^{(j)}, {\mathbf T}^{(j)}$ from 2D correspondences $\mathbf{p}^{(j)}_i$.

concepts.title: Scale drift

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: The accumulation of slight numerical errors in scale factor when adding new images to a 3D reconstruction over time.
concepts.content: When every point is not visible in every view, each new image added to a structure from motion (SFM) reconstruction must be triangulated with respect to its closest image. In doing so, slight numerical errors may occur, causing the new frame to have an ever-so-slightly different scale factor with respect to the reconstruction. This error accumulates over time, causing scale drift.
concepts.motivation_md: Scale drift is a critical problem in incremental SFM and SLAM because it leads to geometric inconsistencies where the reconstructed scene's size and distances become distorted over long sequences.
concepts.recap_md: - Occurs when new frames are triangulated with slight numerical errors in scale.

concepts.title: Bundle adjustment

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: The process of optimizing the 'bundle of rays' connecting camera centers and 3D point coordinates to minimize reprojection error.
concepts.content: Bundle adjustment refers to the process of optimizing the "bundle of rays" connecting the camera centers and the coordinates of the 3D points. It is also described as the optimization of the reprojection error.
concepts.motivation_md: Bundle adjustment is used to refine initial 3D reconstructions and camera poses, ensuring that the final model is as consistent as possible with all observed 2D image data.
concepts.recap_md: - Optimizes the reprojection error of a 3D reconstruction.

concepts.title: Interest points

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Image locations that are likely to be stable under different geometric transformations and illumination changes.
concepts.content: The goal of finding image features is to locate image locations that are likely to be stable under different sets of geometric transformations (translation, scaling, rotation, skew, and projective) and illumination changes. These stable regions are called interest points.
concepts.motivation_md: Interest points provide reliable landmarks in an image that can be matched across different views, which is a prerequisite for tasks like 3D reconstruction and object recognition.
concepts.recap_md: - Stable image regions used as features for matching across views.

concepts.title: Moving element

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: An early term for interest points, referring to any image point that could be identified and followed over time.
concepts.content: Initially, interest points were called moving elements. A moving element was defined as any image point that could be identified and followed over time, such as a corner, a line termination point, or a texture element.

concepts.title: Interest point detection

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Interest point detection identifies image regions that are distinct from their surroundings and stable under geometric transformations to facilitate stereo matching and 3D reconstruction.
concepts.content:
Interest point detection identifies image regions, such as corners, that are likely to be distinct from their surroundings and stable under geometric transformations. Classical methods include the Harris corner detector, local extrema of the Laplacian pyramid across space and scale, Harris-Laplace, and maximally stable regions. 

More recently, detecting points of interest has been formulated as a learning problem. Given a set of manually annotated examples, a classifier can be trained to automatically label image patches as being centered on a keypoint or not. Examples of learning-based approaches include Quad-Networks and SuperPoint. 

(see figure: Keypoint detector formulated as a patch classification problem. The classifier labels the patch as containing a keypoint in the center or not.)

(see figure: All the detected keypoints in three views from the sugar bowl. But the images look rather textureless; what is the keypoint detector finding interesting in these images?)

Training a classifier often involves using synthetic images where keypoints are unambiguously defined or augmenting real images with random geometric transformations to create robust ground truth. As shown in the sugar bowl and plaza examples, keypoint detectors find image regions with strong spatial changes, such as window corners, bricks, or even small surface irregularities on seemingly textureless objects.

[FIGURE:20cc53bc83ed338f]

[FIGURE:549e4ecf64ea35ae]

While hand-engineered detectors are derived from first principles and require no training data, learning-based detectors can leverage unsupervised learning to achieve state-of-the-art performance.
concepts.motivation_md: To perform 3D reconstruction or stereo matching, a system must first identify specific locations in an image that can be reliably found again from a different perspective. Interest point detection solves this by finding 'anchors' like corners or textures that remain recognizable despite changes in camera angle or lighting.

key_passage.text: Corners are examples of image regions that are likely to be distinct from the image surroundings and also be stable under geometric transformations (i.e., corners remain corners under a number of transformations).

concepts.title: Local image descriptors

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Local image descriptors are numerical vectors extracted at keypoint locations to uniquely identify and match those points across different images.
concepts.content:
Once a keypoint detector finds stable image regions, a local image descriptor is extracted at each location to allow finding the same keypoint across different images. Classical hand-engineered descriptors include SIFT, SURF, and ORB. 

(see figure: Examples of descriptors for three keypoints. For each keypoint, the figure shows the corresponding image patch and the computed descriptor. Each descriptor has a length of 256 values.)

These descriptors represent the image patch around a keypoint as a vector (e.g., of length 256). This representation allows for matching keypoints even under different viewpoints and illumination conditions. For instance, a descriptor can identify the same window corner or surface irregularity across multiple views of a scene.

[FIGURE:867b7d3bf524344c]

[FIGURE:79782851e8d2b5ec]
concepts.motivation_md: Detecting a keypoint is not enough; the system needs a way to 'describe' that point so it can be mathematically compared to points in other images. Descriptors provide a unique signature for each point, enabling the matching process required for 3D reconstruction.
concepts.recap_md: - Descriptors are vectors that characterize the visual information in an image patch around a keypoint.

We need now to extract at each location a descriptor that will allow finding the same keypoint across the different images.

concepts.title: Brute-force matching

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Brute-force matching compares features from one image with features from every other image in a dataset.
concepts.content: Brute-force matching is a procedure where features from one image are matched with features from every other image in the set. This approach is typically used when the total number of images is small. Modern implementations may utilize graph network-based matchers, such as SuperGlue, to perform the actual matching of these features.
concepts.motivation_md: When the relationship between images is unknown, the simplest way to find correspondences is to compare every feature in one image against every feature in all others. This ensures no potential matches are missed when the dataset size allows for such computation.
concepts.recap_md: - Matches features by comparing every image pair in the dataset.

concepts.title: Incremental Structure from Motion Optimization

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Incremental Structure from Motion builds a 3D reconstruction by starting with an image pair and sequentially adding images while refining camera poses and point locations.
concepts.content:
Incremental Structure from Motion (SFM) minimizes reprojection error by building a reconstruction step-by-step. The process typically starts with a pair of images, using their matches to compute fundamental and essential matrices while accounting for outliers via RANSAC. An initial 3D reconstruction is created through triangulation. 

Additional images are then added sequentially, repeating the matching and triangulation process until all images are incorporated. This results in an initial set of approximated camera poses and 3D locations for keypoints. Finally, the camera poses, 3D locations, and intrinsics are refined using bundle adjustment, often employing a robust cost function like the Huber kernel to handle errors.
concepts.motivation_md: Solving for all camera positions and 3D points simultaneously is computationally difficult and prone to failure. By starting small and adding images one by one, the system can maintain a stable estimate of the scene and filter out errors early in the process.
concepts.recap_md: - Starts with a base image pair to establish an initial 3D triangulation.

key_passage.text: One standard approach is to do it incrementally starting with only a pair of images. We use the matches between those two images to compute the fundamental and essential matrices, while accounting for outliers using RANSAC. We can then compute an initial 3D reconstruction of the matched points using triangulation as we have already discussed in Then, we add another image and we repeat the same process until we have incorporated all the images.

motivation.text: To find the final set of 3D points, the camera poses and the 3D locations of the keypoints are then further refined by bundle adjustment (camera intrinsics are refined too, if needed).

slots.example:
Incremental Structure from Motion (SFM) minimizes reprojection error by building a reconstruction step-by-step. The process typically starts with a pair of images, using their matches to compute fundamental and essential matrices while accounting for outliers via RANSAC. An initial 3D reconstruction is created through triangulation. 

Additional images are then added sequentially, repeating the matching and triangulation process until all images are incorporated. This results in an initial set of approximated camera poses and 3D locations for keypoints. Finally, the camera poses, 3D locations, and intrinsics are refined using bundle adjustment, often employing a robust cost function like the Huber kernel to handle errors.

concepts.title: Batch-mode Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Batch-mode Structure from Motion computes the entire scene structure and camera poses offline after all input images have been processed.
concepts.content: Batch-mode Structure from Motion (SFM) is an offline approach that computes the scene structure after processing all input images. In this mode, bundle adjustment is typically run only once, though it must handle a potentially large number of cameras and 3D points simultaneously. This approach leverages information from all available viewpoints from the start. However, a significant drawback is that if new images are added to the set, the entire SFM pipeline must be rerun from the beginning.
concepts.motivation_md: Batch-mode SFM is ideal for situations where all images are available upfront (like a photo collection) and the highest possible global consistency is desired, as it optimizes all parameters together rather than sequentially.
concepts.recap_md: - Processes all images simultaneously to compute scene structure.

concepts.title: Incremental-mode Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Incremental-mode Structure from Motion estimates scene structure and camera parameters sequentially as new images arrive.
concepts.content: Incremental-mode Structure from Motion (SFM), also known as online SFM, attempts to estimate scene structure and camera parameters as each new image arrives. In this mode, bundle adjustment is performed periodically whenever a sufficient number of new points have been added. This approach is particularly useful for applications where the full set of images is not available beforehand or where real-time performance is a requirement.
concepts.motivation_md: For applications like robotics or augmented reality, the system cannot wait for all data to be collected. Incremental SFM allows the reconstruction to grow and update dynamically as the camera moves through an environment.
concepts.recap_md: - Updates the 3D model and camera parameters as new images are provided.

key_passage.text: Online, or incremental-mode SFM approaches attempt to estimate scene structure and camera parameters as and when a new image arrives. In this mode, bundle adjustment is run periodically, whenever a sufficient number of points have been newly added.

motivation.text: Incremental-mode SFM is often used in applications where all images are not available a priori, or where real-time performance is desired.

concepts.title: Sparse Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Sparse Structure from Motion computes 3D reconstructions for a small subset of distinct, reliably detectable image pixels.
concepts.content: Sparse Structure from Motion (SFM) is a feature-based variant where 3D reconstruction is computed only for a small subset of image pixels. These pixels correspond to distinct points that can be detected reliably and repeatably across different camera poses. While some approaches attempt to use lines, planes, or objects, point-based features remain the most popular choice due to their geometric simplicity and the wide availability of robust detectors and descriptors.
concepts.motivation_md: Computing 3D coordinates for every single pixel is computationally expensive and often unnecessary. Sparse SFM focuses only on the most 'reliable' points (like corners), which provides enough information to determine camera motion and the basic geometry of the scene efficiently.
concepts.recap_md: - Reconstructs only a subset of distinct points rather than the full image.

key_passage.text: In sparse SFM, the 3D reconstruction is computed only for a small subset of the image pixels --- distinct points that may be detected reliably and repeatably across camera pose variations.

motivation.text: Point-based features remain the most popular choice due to their geometric simplicity, and the availability of a wide range of point feature detectors and descriptors.

concepts.title: Dense Structure from Motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Dense Structure from Motion computes a 3D reconstruction for nearly every pixel in an image by optimizing photometric error.
concepts.content:
In dense Structure from Motion (SFM), 3D reconstruction is computed for every (or most) image pixels, resulting in rich and visually informative models useful for robot navigation or mixed reality. Unlike sparse methods that minimize 3D reprojection error of features, dense SFM approaches usually optimize photometric error—the difference in intensity (grayscale or RGB) of corresponding pixels across images. 

These techniques are generally slower than sparse methods and require more assumptions, such as the scene being Lambertian (intensity is invariant to viewing direction). They also typically handle smaller baseline motions between images compared to point feature-based approaches.
concepts.motivation_md: While sparse SFM gives a 'skeleton' of a scene, dense SFM provides a complete surface reconstruction. This is essential for tasks like obstacle avoidance in robotics or placing virtual objects in mixed reality where the full geometry of the environment matters.
concepts.recap_md: - Computes 3D data for almost every pixel to create detailed reconstructions.

key_passage.text: In dense SFM, the 3D reconstruction is computed for every (or most) of the image pixels. The resulting 3D reconstructions are rich and visually informative, and are useful in applications like robot navigation or mixed reality.

concepts.title: Multiview geometry

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Multiview geometry is the study of reconstructing 3D objects or scenes from multiple 2D images.
concepts.content: Multiview geometry studies the 3D reconstruction of an object or a scene from multiple viewpoints.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how multiple 2D projections of the same scene relate to each other is fundamental for recovering the 3D structure of the world from images.
concepts.recap_md:
- Multiview geometry focuses on the mathematical relationship between different camera views of the same 3D scene.
- It provides the foundation for techniques like Structure from Motion and stereo vision.

concepts.title: Biological motion

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Biological motion refers to the characteristic patterns of movement exhibited by living organisms.
concepts.content: Biological motion is a term introduced by Swedish psychologist Gunnaar Johansson to describe the typical motion of biological organisms, based on his work on gestalt laws of motion perception.
concepts.motivation_md: Humans have a specialized ability to recognize living beings and their actions from very sparse motion cues, which is a key area of study in both psychology and computer vision.
concepts.recap_md:
- The term was coined by Gunnaar Johansson to describe the unique motion patterns of living things.
- It highlights the human ability to perceive complex structures from motion alone.

concepts.title: Structure from Motion (SFM)

position.chapter_title: Multiview Geometry and Structure from Motion

concepts.one_liner: Structure from Motion is the process of estimating 3D structures from a sequence of 2D images by assuming the objects are rigid.
concepts.content: Structure from Motion (SFM) is the mathematical formulation of 3D reconstruction from camera motion, largely advanced by the rigidity assumption. This assumption states that any set of elements undergoing a 2D transformation that can be uniquely interpreted as a rigid body moving in space should be interpreted as such. Most SFM methods represent a sequence using the temporal trajectories of a sparse set of points, known as sparse SFM. (see figure: Early illustrations on the perceptual power of motion. (a) Nested cylinders by Shimon Ullman, 1979, illustrated how rigid motion elicits a strong 3D interpretation. (b) One frame from the point-light...)
concepts.motivation_md: SFM allows for the creation of 3D models from simple video sequences or collections of photos, which is vital for mapping, special effects, and robotics.
concepts.recap_md:
- SFM relies on the rigidity assumption to interpret 2D image changes as 3D motion and structure.
- Sparse SFM typically uses the trajectories of specific points over time as input for reconstruction.

key_passage.text: Any set of elements undergoing a two dimensional transformation which has a unique interpretation as a rigid body moving in space should be interpreted as such a body in motion.

motivation.text: One major advance that allowed writing a mathematical formulation of the problem of structure from motion (SFM) was the rigidity assumption introduced by Shimon Ullman in 1979. Since then, the 3D reconstruction of rigid objects from camera motion has been a rich area of work.

prereq.rationale: Sparse SFM is a specific implementation of the general Structure from Motion problem focused on recovering 3D structure and camera poses from image sets.
Scale drift is a specific error accumulation problem that occurs during the incremental addition of images in SFM.
Interest point detection is the technical process of identifying the stable regions defined as interest points.
Descriptors are numerical representations extracted specifically at the locations of detected interest points.
Brute-force matching operates by comparing the local image descriptors extracted from different images.
Bundle adjustment is the final refinement step in the incremental SFM pipeline to optimize camera poses and 3D points.
Incremental SFM relies on periodic bundle adjustment to refine scene structure and camera parameters as new images are added.
Sparse SFM depends on the detection of distinct and repeatable interest points across different camera poses.
The points used in sparse SFM are typically identified and matched using robust detectors and descriptors.
The rigidity assumption is presented as the fundamental principle underlying the structure from motion problem.
This algorithm provides a concrete method for solving the SFM problem for rigid bodies.

overlay.rationale: Moving elements was the historical term for what are now called interest points.
Batch-mode SFM processes all images simultaneously offline, whereas incremental SFM builds the reconstruction step-by-step.
Incremental SFM is a specific sequential mode of the broader Structure from Motion task, designed for online processing.
Incremental SFM processes images sequentially for real-time needs, whereas batch mode requires the entire image set beforehand.
Sparse SFM is a feature-based variant of Structure from Motion that reconstructs only a subset of image pixels.
Dense SFM is a variant of Structure from Motion that aims to reconstruct nearly every pixel in an image.
Dense SFM is often contrasted with sparse methods because it optimizes photometric error rather than reprojection error.
SFM is a specific instance of multiview geometry where the multiple views are obtained through motion.
General multiview SFM expands the scope of traditional SFM from a single moving camera to arbitrary collections of images.
